newsitem.title: JAPAN: Honda's profits rev up, Mazda gets back on track.
newsitem.headline: Honda's profits rev up, Mazda gets back on track.

text.p: Honda Motor Co drove into the profits fast lane on Friday, while Mazda Motor Corp got back on track, posting a modest profit for the half-year under the leadership of its new foreign boss.

Honda, which has lately been shedding its image as a maker of sporty cars for that of a RV company, unveiled a record parent current profit of 69.2 billion yen ($623 million) for the six months to September, four times higher than the year earlier period.
"The domestic car market is better than expected, and we got help from the weaker yen," Yoshihide Munekuni, executive vice president of the third-ranked automaker told reporters.
Mazda, Japan's fifth-largest car maker, also benefited from the weak yen, which makes Japanese goods more cost-competitive abroad.

After a string of first-half losses, Mazda announced that it managed a parent current profit of 2.08 billion yen ($18.7 million) for the six months to the end of September, a boost for its new president, the first foreigner to head a major Japanese firm.
Wallace, a Briton, took the wheel at Mazda in June, soon after Ford Motor Co raised its holding in the company to a one-third stake from the previous 25 percent, giving it management control.

Mazda, whose range of models has failed to excite Japanese customers at a time when its competitors are coming up with a host of popular new models, had posted first-half losses for three straight years.

Honda, meanwhile, has been benefiting from a recreational vehicle (RV) boom in Japan. The popularity of RVs, which now account for about half of Honda's car sales in Japan, helped raise the company's vehicle sales for the April-September period by 22.3 percent from a year earlier.

Honda's Odyssey minivan, which made its debut in October 1994 and triggered Japan's current boom in minivans, is still enjoying strong sales. All of the company's new RVs -- the CR-V light sport-utility vehicle, Orthia station wagon and Step Wagon eight-seat minivan -- are seeing good demand in Japan.

Honda also expects record parent current profits of 155 billion yen ($1.39 billion) for the full year, up from an August estimate of 120 billion yen ($1.08 billion). Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses or gains on non-operating activities.

Mazda said it would enjoy a parent current profit of 11 billion yen ($99.0 million) this fiscal year, almost nine times higher than last year, but the figure was still lower than its May estimate of 25 billion yen ($225 million).

Analysts said Mazda's full-year figure would be helped by the weaker yen, which makes Japanese exports more competitive abroad. A dollar rise by one yen translates into three billion yen ($27.0 million) of annual profits for Mazda, analysts said. The dollar stood at around 111 yen on Friday, against 100 yen a year ago.
But on a group basis, Mazda said it would suffer a net loss of four billion yen ($36.0 million) for the full year, lowering its May forecast of a net profit of 10 billion yen ($90.0 million).
